title: Product Sales Analysis I
statement:
Two tables record sales and the products sold:

- `Sales(sale_id, product_id, year, quantity, price)`: one row per sale in a year; the pair `(sale_id, year)` is unique, so one `sale_id` can appear in several years. `price` is the price of one unit. Every `product_id` exists in `Product`.
- `Product(product_id, product_name)`: one row per product; `product_id` is unique.

For every row of `Sales`, report the product's name, the sale's year and its unit price, as the columns `product_name`, `year` and `price`. Products that were never sold do not appear. Rows may come in any order.
reference:
SELECT p.product_name, s.year, s.price
FROM Sales AS s
JOIN Product AS p
  ON p.product_id = s.product_id;
brute:
SELECT
  (SELECT product_name FROM Product WHERE Product.product_id = Sales.product_id) AS product_name,
  year,
  price
FROM Sales
notes:
## Intuition

`Sales` already holds the year and the price; only the product's name lives elsewhere, in `Product`. Each sale points at exactly one product through `product_id`, and that id always exists, so an **inner join** on `product_id` attaches the right name to every sale and drops nothing. Products that were never sold have no matching sale and simply do not appear.

## Approach

1. Read from `Sales` (alias `s`): every output row comes from one sale.
2. `JOIN Product` (alias `p`) on `p.product_id = s.product_id` to find each sale's product.
3. Select `p.product_name`, `s.year` and `s.price`, keeping repeated rows: two sales of the same product in the same year at the same price are two output rows.

## Example 1, step by step

- Sale 1 (product 100, 2008, 5000) joins Nokia, giving `(Nokia, 2008, 5000)`.
- Sale 2 (product 100, 2009, 5000) also joins Nokia, giving `(Nokia, 2009, 5000)`.
- Sale 7 (product 200, 2011, 9000) joins Apple, giving `(Apple, 2011, 9000)`.
- Samsung (300) has no sale, so it never appears.

## Complexity

- Time: O(S + P) for S sales and P products with a hash or index on `Product.product_id`, its primary key.
- Space: O(S) for the result.

## Pitfalls

- Starting from `Product` with a left join reports unsold products with null years and prices.
- `SELECT DISTINCT` merges different sales that share a product, year and price; each sale is its own row.
- `price` is the unit price, so it is reported as is; multiplying by `quantity` answers a different question.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `s` | `Sales`, one row per sale and per output row |
| `p` | `Product`, joined to give each sale its product's name |
| `JOIN ... ON` | matches a sale to its product through `product_id` |

narration.1: Choose the three output columns: the name from Product, the year and unit price from Sales.
narration.2: Sales drives the query, so every sale produces one row.
narration.3: An inner join is enough: every sale names a product that exists, and unsold products should not appear.
narration.4: Each sale is matched with its product through product_id.
